author: A Robot
objectives: Identify the structural components of DNA — the sugar-phosphate backbone, the four nitrogenous bases, and hydrogen bonds between base pairs — and describe how they assemble into the double helix.
Apply complementary base-pairing rules (A-T, G-C) to determine a complementary strand sequence and explain why A-T forms two hydrogen bonds while G-C forms three.
Describe the antiparallel orientation of DNA strands and explain how the 5'-to-3' directionality of each backbone determines it.
Trace the action of helicase, single-strand binding proteins, DNA polymerase, and DNA ligase at the replication fork.

Explain why replication produces a continuously synthesized leading strand and a discontinuous lagging strand of Okazaki fragments, relating this to unidirectional 5'-to-3' polymerase activity on antiparallel templates.
Articulate why DNA replication is semiconservative and predict daughter-molecule composition after one and two rounds of replication.

modules.moduleName: Scene 1: The Double Helix and Its Components
modules.description: A guided tour of the three-dimensional structure of DNA — the antiparallel sugar-phosphate backbones, the four nitrogenous bases projecting inward, and how they assemble into the double helix.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the sugar-phosphate backbone, nitrogenous bases, and hydrogen bonds within the double helix.
Describe how two antiparallel strands spiral around a common axis.
Relate the 5'-to-3' directionality of each backbone to the antiparallel arrangement of the strands.
instructions: Use Next and Previous to move through the scene.
Observe the rotating helix and note where the backbones and bases are located.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce the intact rotating double helix so students can view the overall three-dimensional spiral shape before components are labeled.
clips.narration: Welcome. This is DNA — deoxyribonucleic acid — shown as a three-dimensional double helix. Two long strands spiral around a common central axis, like a twisted ladder. Let's take it apart to see what it's made of.

clips.changeMeaning: Reveal the backbone label and tint the helix to emphasize the two spiraling sugar-phosphate rails that form the sides of the ladder.
clips.narration: Each side of the ladder is a sugar-phosphate backbone: alternating deoxyribose sugars and phosphate groups. These two backbones run in opposite directions and form the structural rails of the molecule.

clips.changeMeaning: Reveal the bases label and re-tint the helix toward warm base colors to shift attention to the nitrogenous bases projecting inward as the ladder rungs.
clips.narration: Projecting inward from the backbones are the four nitrogenous bases: adenine, thymine, guanine, and cytosine. They form the rungs of the ladder, meeting in the middle of the helix.

clips.changeMeaning: Reveal the directionality label and slow the rotation so students can focus on the antiparallel 5'-to-3' orientation of the two strands.
clips.narration: Notice the arrows: one strand runs five-prime to three-prime, while its partner runs three-prime to five-prime. Because the backbone has a built-in direction, the two strands must be antiparallel — a fact that becomes critical during replication.

modules.description: A close-up of a single base-pair rung showing the complementary pairing rules and the hydrogen bonds that hold the strands together — two for A-T and three for G-C.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Apply the complementary base-pairing rules (A with T, G with C).
Explain why A-T forms two hydrogen bonds and G-C forms three.
Predict a complementary strand sequence from a given strand.
instructions: Step through the clips to compare the two types of base pairs.
Count the hydrogen bonds shown between each pair.

clips.changeMeaning: Show the isolated adenine and thymine bases approaching each other to set up the concept of a single complementary pairing.
clips.narration: The bases don't pair randomly. Adenine always pairs with thymine, and guanine always pairs with cytosine. Here we have adenine and thymine facing each other.

clips.changeMeaning: Reveal the two hydrogen bonds between A and T to show the specific number and strength of the A-T interaction.
clips.narration: Adenine and thymine are held together by two hydrogen bonds. Two bonds — a relatively weaker, easily separated pairing.

clips.changeMeaning: Bring in guanine and cytosine below the A-T pair and reveal three hydrogen bonds to contrast the stronger G-C interaction.
clips.narration: Now guanine and cytosine. This pair is held by three hydrogen bonds, making G-C pairing stronger and more thermally stable than A-T. The shapes and bonding chemistry are why these specific partners always match.

modules.moduleName: Scene 3: Semiconservative Replication at the Fork
modules.description: A dynamic walkthrough of DNA replication: helicase unwinds the helix, single-strand binding proteins stabilize the strands, and DNA polymerase builds a continuous leading strand and a discontinuous lagging strand joined by ligase — illustrating why replication is semiconservative.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace the roles of helicase, single-strand binding proteins, DNA polymerase, and DNA ligase.
Explain the difference between leading and lagging strand synthesis and Okazaki fragments.
Explain why replication is semiconservative and predict daughter-strand composition.
instructions: Advance through the clips to watch the replication fork open and new strands form.
Track which strand is continuous and which is built in fragments.

components.text: Semiconservative: 1 old strand + 1 new strand per daughter

clips.changeMeaning: Present the intact replication fork region and introduce helicase moving to the fork to begin unwinding the double helix.
clips.narration: Replication begins when the enzyme helicase reaches the double helix and unwinds it, breaking the hydrogen bonds between base pairs. This opens a Y-shaped region called the replication fork.

clips.changeMeaning: Add single-strand binding proteins coating the exposed strands to show how the unwound template is stabilized and kept from re-annealing.
clips.narration: As the strands separate, single-strand binding proteins coat the exposed template, keeping the two strands apart and preventing them from snapping back together.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce DNA polymerase on the leading-strand template moving continuously toward the fork to illustrate continuous 5'-to-3' synthesis.
clips.narration: DNA polymerase now reads each template and adds nucleotides, but only in the five-prime to three-prime direction. On the leading strand, this direction follows the fork, so polymerase synthesizes one continuous new strand.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce lagging-strand polymerase synthesizing away from the fork in short Okazaki fragments to demonstrate the discontinuous synthesis forced by antiparallel templates.
clips.narration: The other template runs the opposite way. Because polymerase can still only build five-prime to three-prime, the lagging strand is made in short pieces called Okazaki fragments, synthesized backward, away from the fork.

clips.changeMeaning: Bring in DNA ligase to seal the Okazaki fragments, completing the lagging strand and connecting the fragments into one continuous strand.
clips.narration: DNA ligase then seals the gaps between Okazaki fragments, stitching them into one continuous lagging strand.

clips.changeMeaning: Reveal the semiconservative summary label and re-tint the fork to show each daughter molecule contains one parental and one new strand.
clips.narration: Each daughter molecule ends up with one original parental strand and one brand-new strand. That is why replication is called semiconservative. After one round you have two such hybrids; after two rounds, only two of the four molecules still contain an original strand.
